### Problem: Pairs of Songs With Total Durations Divisible by 60 {#sec-cnt-p2-songs}

::: {.p-statement}
`time[i]` is the duration in seconds of the $i$-th song. Return the number of pairs $(i, j)$ with $i < j$ and $(time[i] + time[j]) \bmod 60 = 0$.

For `time = [30,20,150,100,40]` the answer is $3$: $(0,2)$ totals $180$, $(1,3)$ totals $120$, $(1,4)$ totals $60$. For `time = [60,60,60]` every pair works, so the answer is $3$.

Constraints: $1 \le n \le 6 \cdot 10^4$, $1 \le time[i] \le 500$.

Source: [LC 1010 · Pairs of Songs With Total Durations Divisible by 60](https://leetcode.com/problems/pairs-of-songs-with-total-durations-divisible-by-60/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The relation is no longer "equal values" — it is "the two values add to a multiple of $60$". Everything from @sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs still applies, with one change of currency: **only the remainders matter**. $(a+b) \bmod 60 = 0 \iff (a \bmod 60) + (b \bmod 60) \in \{0, 60\}$, so a duration of $150$ and a duration of $30$ are the same player. That collapses an unbounded value domain into $60$ buckets, which is the move @sec-cnt-a5 teaches in general: when the number of distinguishable states is small, count over states instead of over items.

Now the right-end tally from rung 2 of @sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs needs only one edit. When the cursor reaches a song with remainder $r$, a partner is any earlier song with remainder $60 - r$ — except that $60 - 0 = 60$ is not a slot, so the lookup is `need = (60 - r) % 60`, which folds remainder $0$ onto itself. Read the sample `time = [30,20,150,100,40]` that way:

| song | remainder | complement looked up | earlier copies | running answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 30 | 30 | 0 | 0 |
| 20 | 20 | 40 | 0 | 0 |
| 150 | 30 | 30 | 1 | 1 |
| 100 | 40 | 20 | 1 | 2 |
| 40 | 40 | 20 | 1 | 3 |

Total $3$, the sample. The histogram is $\{20:1,\; 30:2,\; 40:2\}$, and the third rung reads the same answer straight off it: bucket $20$ pairs with bucket $40$ giving $1 \times 2 = 2$, and bucket $30$ pairs with **itself** giving $\binom{2}{2} = 1$, so $2 + 1 = 3$.

Those self-complements are the one place where the bucket view needs care. A bucket $r$ is its own partner exactly when $2r \equiv 0 \pmod{60}$, i.e. $r \in \{0, 30\}$ — the two halves of the modulus. For every other remainder you must count the pair of buckets $(r, 60-r)$ **once**, which is why the sweep below only visits $r \le 60 - r$. With $n$ up to $6 \cdot 10^4$, the naive double loop would examine $\binom{60000}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$ pairs: the reason this problem is Medium and not Easy.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test every pair.** Two loops and one modulo. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space — correct, and roughly $1.8 \cdot 10^9$ iterations at the limit, so it times out.
2. **One pass over 60 buckets.** Keep the count of each remainder seen so far and add `hist[(60 - r) % 60]` as you go. $O(n)$ time, $O(60)$ space. The intended solution.
3. **Pair whole buckets at once (histogram).** Build the histogram first, then walk $r = 0 \ldots 30$: self-complementary buckets contribute $\binom{c}{2}$, all others contribute $c_r \cdot c_{60-r}$. Same complexity, no order dependence — and the form that generalises to "how many pairs satisfy a relation on residues".
:::

::: {#fig-cnt-p2-songs}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
sg_hist = [0] * 60
for sg_t in [30, 20, 150, 100, 40]:
    sg_hist[sg_t % 60] += 1
sg_cols = [0, 20, 30, 40]                      # every non-empty bucket, plus bucket 0
sg_pairs = []
for sg_r in sg_cols:
    sg_c = (60 - sg_r) % 60
    if sg_c == sg_r:
        sg_pairs.append(str(sg_hist[sg_r] * (sg_hist[sg_r] - 1) // 2))
    elif sg_r < sg_c:
        sg_pairs.append(str(sg_hist[sg_r] * sg_hist[sg_c]))
    else:
        sg_pairs.append("(with 20)")           # bucket pair already credited at r = 20
assert sg_pairs == ["0", "2", "1", "(with 20)"]
assert sum(int(x) for x in sg_pairs[:3]) == 3
assert [r for r in range(60) if sg_hist[r]] == [20, 30, 40]


def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["remainder r", *map(str, sg_cols)],
                   ["songs at r", *(str(sg_hist[r]) for r in sg_cols)],
                   ["partner (60-r)%60", *(str((60 - r) % 60) for r in sg_cols)],
                   ["pairs credited", *sg_pairs]],
           colors={(1, 2): "cyan", (1, 4): "cyan", (2, 3): "amber", (2, 1): "amber",
                   (3, 2): "green", (3, 3): "green"},
           cell_w=1.6)
V.show(draw)
```

Only three of the sixty buckets are non-empty here: $20$, $30$ and $40$ (the other $56$ hold no song and credit nothing). Bucket $20$ and bucket $40$ are complements (cyan) and contribute $1 \times 2 = 2$ pairs, credited once at $r = 20$; the two amber partners are the self-complementary buckets $0$ and $30$. Bucket $30$ pairs within itself, $\binom{2}{2} = 1$, and bucket $0$ (songs that are already a multiple of $60$) is empty in this sample, so it credits $\binom{0}{2} = 0$. Total $2 + 1 = 3$.

:::

#### Test every pair

::: {.form-next}
The definition: every $i < j$, one modulo test. $O(n^2)$ time and $O(1)$ space. Keep it as the oracle for the two faster rungs, and note how few pairs actually pass — $3$ out of $10$ on the first sample.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("songs", "scan")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def song_scan(time):
    ans = 0
    for i in range(len(time)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(time)):
            if (time[i] + time[j]) % 60 == 0:
                ans += 1
    return ans


assert song_scan([30, 20, 150, 100, 40]) == 3
assert song_scan([60, 60, 60]) == 3
assert song_scan([20, 100]) == 1
assert song_scan([10]) == 0
```

##### C++

```cpp
int songScan(vector<int>& time) {
    int ans = 0, n = time.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
            if ((time[i] + time[j]) % 60 == 0) ++ans;
    return ans;
}
```
:::

#### One pass over 60 buckets

::: {.form-next}
Replace the value by its remainder, then run the right-end tally: a new song pairs with every earlier song in the complementary bucket. $O(n)$ time, and the table is a fixed $60$ cells — no hash map, no sorting, no dependence on the duration range.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("songs", "rem60")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def song_bucket(time):
    hist = [0] * 60
    ans = 0
    for t in time:
        r = t % 60
        ans += hist[(60 - r) % 60]         # the % 60 folds r = 0 onto itself
        hist[r] += 1
    return ans


assert song_bucket([30, 20, 150, 100, 40]) == 3
assert song_bucket([60, 60, 60]) == 3      # 0 + 1 + 2 as the bucket fills
assert song_bucket([20, 100]) == 1
# remainder 0 must not reach for a slot 60: with a 61-wide table and a bare
# `60 - r`, multiples of 60 would look up an always-empty bucket
padded = [0] * 61
lost = 0
for t in [60, 120, 60]:
    r = t % 60
    lost += padded[60 - r]                  # padded[60] is never written
    padded[r] += 1
assert lost == 0                            # ... so the answer silently becomes 0
assert song_bucket([60, 120, 60]) == 3      # (0,1), (0,2), (1,2)
for _ in range(150):
    a = [random.randint(1, 500) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 25))]
    assert song_bucket(a) == song_scan(a)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int songBucket(vector<int>& time) {
    vector<int> hist(60, 0);
    int ans = 0;
    for (int t : time) {
        int r = t % 60;
        ans += hist[(60 - r) % 60];         // (60 - 0) % 60 == 0
        ++hist[r];
    }
    return ans;
}
```
:::

#### Pair whole buckets at once (histogram)

::: {.form-next}
Build the histogram, then credit each *pair of buckets* in one multiplication. Order stops mattering, which makes it easier to prove right and easier to adapt when the question is about residues rather than about positions.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("songs", "hist")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def song_hist(time):
    hist = [0] * 60
    for t in time:
        hist[t % 60] += 1
    ans = 0
    for r in range(31):                     # r <= 60 - r: each bucket pair once
        c = 60 - r if r else 0              # 0 and 30 are self-complementary
        if c == r:
            ans += hist[r] * (hist[r] - 1) // 2
        else:
            ans += hist[r] * hist[c]
    return ans


assert song_hist([30, 20, 150, 100, 40]) == 3
assert song_hist([60, 60, 60]) == 3
# the sample histogram and the two kinds of credit
h = [0] * 60
for t in [30, 20, 150, 100, 40]:
    h[t % 60] += 1
assert (h[20], h[30], h[40]) == (1, 2, 2)
assert h[20] * h[40] == 2 and h[30] * (h[30] - 1) // 2 == 1
# the self-complementary remainders are exactly 0 and 30
assert [r for r in range(60) if (2 * r) % 60 == 0] == [0, 30]
for _ in range(150):
    a = [random.randint(1, 500) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 25))]
    assert song_hist(a) == song_bucket(a) == song_scan(a)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int songHist(vector<int>& time) {
    vector<int> hist(60, 0);
    for (int t : time) ++hist[t % 60];
    long long ans = 0;                        // hist[0] * (hist[0] - 1) can pass 2^31
    for (int r = 0; r <= 30; ++r) {           // r <= 60 - r: count each pair once
        int c = (60 - r) % 60;
        if (c == r) ans += 1LL * hist[r] * (hist[r] - 1) / 2;
        else        ans += 1LL * hist[r] * hist[c];
    }
    return (int)ans;                          // the final count is at most C(60000, 2) < 2^31
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(n^2)$ for the double loop ($\binom{60000}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$ tests at the limit — far past the time budget); $O(n)$ for the bucket sweep and $O(n + 60)$ for the histogram. **Space** $O(1)$ beyond the input for the naive rung, $O(60) = O(1)$ for both fast rungs — a fixed 60-cell table, independent of $n$ and of the duration range $[1,500]$. **Width of the answer** at most $\binom{6 \cdot 10^4}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$, which fits in a 32-bit `int` (ceiling $2{,}147{,}483{,}647$) with only about $16\%$ to spare — so `int` is legal here but a `long long` accumulator costs nothing and saves you the moment $n$ grows.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$: no pair, answer $0$; the sweep reads an empty histogram.
- Every duration a multiple of $60$: all songs land in bucket $0$, so the answer is $\binom{n}{2}$ — `[60,60,60]` $\to$ $3$, matching the second sample.
- Remainder $0$ is the special case: `60 - r` is out of range exactly there, which is what the `% 60` in `(60 - r) % 60` is for. The cell above shows the failure mode: with the bare `60 - r` and a padded table, `[60,120,60]` answers $0$ instead of $3$.
- Durations at the top of the range ($500 \bmod 60 = 20$) need no extra bucket: every remainder $0 \ldots 59$ is already reachable from $[1,500]$ (the songs $1 \ldots 60$ give them all), so the table is exactly $60$ wide no matter how large the durations get.
- **Debug tip.** An answer that overshoots by $\binom{c}{2} + c$ for a self-complementary bucket means you used $c_r \cdot c_{60-r}$ on the diagonal too — the diagonal term must be $\binom{c}{2}$, not $c^2$. On `[60,60,60]` the mistake gives $9$ instead of $3$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **`need = 60 - r` without the outer modulo.** Fine for $r > 0$, an index error (or a silent wrong bucket in a padded table) for $r = 0$.
- **Counting bucket pairs twice.** Sweeping all $60$ remainders in rung 3 doubles every cross term ($20 \times 40$ and $40 \times 20$); stop at $30$ or halve the total.
- **Using $c^2$ on the diagonal.** Self-complementary buckets have no partner to multiply against; the pairs inside one bucket are $\binom{c}{2}$ because $i < j$.
- **Tallying after the increment.** Adding `hist[need]` *after* `hist[r] += 1` lets a song pair with itself when $r$ is its own complement — on `[60,60,60]` that gives $6$ instead of $3$.
- **Reaching for a hash map of durations.** The durations themselves are irrelevant; two songs with the same remainder are interchangeable for this predicate.
:::

**Variants.** Replace $60$ by an arbitrary $k$ and pairs of songs by pairs of **prefix sums**, and you get LC 974 (subarray sums divisible by $k$): the same $k$-bucket histogram, but the relation becomes *equal* residues, $P[r] \equiv P[l]$, so the lookup is `hist[r]` itself and no bucket needs a partner — that version is worked in @sec-pref-p2. Keeping the right-end tally and changing the relation to "the two prefix sums differ by exactly $goal$" is @sec-cnt-p3-binsum. With an arbitrary even $k$ the self-complementary buckets are $0$ and $k/2$; with odd $k$ only $0$.

- [LC 974 · Subarray Sums Divisible by K](https://leetcode.com/problems/subarray-sums-divisible-by-k/){difficulty="Medium"} — solved in @sec-pref-p2; redo it here from the bucket view and check your answer against the book's.
